questions.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled components: how do they differ and when do you use each?
questions.quick: A controlled input gets its value from React state and reports every change through onChange, so React is the single source of truth. An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM, and I read it through a ref or FormData when I need it. I use controlled inputs when I need live validation, formatting or dependent fields, and uncontrolled ones for simple submit-only forms, file inputs, or very large forms where a render per keystroke is wasteful.
questions.revision: Controlled: value in React state, updated via onChange. Uncontrolled: value lives in the DOM, read through a ref or FormData on demand.

questions.title: When do you lift state up, and when is composition a better fix than prop drilling?
questions.quick: I lift state to the nearest common parent when two siblings need the same value. If the value then has to pass through many components that do not use it, I first try composition: pass the already-built element or a children slot so the intermediate layers never see the props. Only when many distant consumers need the data do I reach for context or a store. I keep state as close as possible to where it is used.
questions.revision: Lift state to the nearest common parent; if props pass through uninterested layers, use children or element props before context or a store.

diagrams.title: Lifting state to a common parent
diagrams.alt: State lives in a parent component. It passes a value and an update callback down to two sibling components, so both always read the same single source of truth.

followUps: What is the downside of lifting state too high?
Why does passing elements as props avoid re-renders?
When would you choose context over composition?

questions.title: What are the common Context API pitfalls around re-renders, and how do you avoid them?
questions.quick: Every component that reads a context re-renders whenever the provider value changes by reference, even if it only uses one field. The classic bug is passing a new object literal as the value on every render. I memoise the value, split contexts by update frequency, separate state from dispatch, and keep fast-changing data out of context. If many consumers need selective subscriptions, I use a store with selectors instead.
questions.revision: Consumers re-render when the context value reference changes. Memoise the value, split contexts, separate state from dispatch, or use a selector-based store.

diagrams.title: Splitting state and dispatch contexts
diagrams.alt: A provider holds reducer state and exposes two contexts. Components that read state re-render on change, while components that only read dispatch do not re-render because dispatch is stable.

followUps: How would a selector-based store avoid these re-renders?
Why is dispatch from useReducer stable?
How do you detect which consumers re-render?

questions.title: How do you design a good custom hook, and what makes one a bad abstraction?
questions.quick: A good custom hook has one clear job, a small and stable API, and hides the wiring such as effects, subscriptions or fetching. I name it useSomething, return a typed tuple or object, accept options rather than many positional arguments, clean up after itself, and keep it free of UI. A bad hook just groups unrelated state to shorten a component, or hides business rules behind a surprising side effect.
questions.revision: One job, small typed API, cleanup included, no UI. Bad hooks bundle unrelated state or hide surprising side effects.
followUps: How do you test a custom hook?
How do custom hooks share state between components?

questions.title: Higher-order components vs render props vs hooks: how do they compare?
questions.quick: All three share logic. A higher-order component wraps a component and returns an enhanced one. A render prop passes a function that the component calls to render with shared data. A hook shares the logic directly inside the component with no extra tree nesting. Today I default to hooks because they compose cleanly and read linearly. I still use HOCs for cross-cutting wrappers such as route guards, and render props for flexible rendering slots.
questions.revision: HOC wraps a component, render props pass a render function, hooks share logic with no nesting. Prefer hooks; keep HOCs for wrappers.
followUps: Why is creating an HOC inside render a bug?
Why are error boundaries still class-based?
What is a headless component?

questions.title: What are error boundaries in React, what do they catch, and where do you place them?
questions.quick: An error boundary is a component that catches errors thrown while rendering its children, in lifecycle methods and in constructors, and shows a fallback instead of unmounting the whole app. It does not catch event handler errors, async code, server rendering or errors in the boundary itself. I place boundaries at route level and around independent widgets, log to a monitoring service, and give users a way to retry.
questions.revision: Boundaries catch render-time errors in the subtree and show a fallback. They miss event handlers and async errors. Place at route and widget level.

diagrams.title: Error boundary containment
diagrams.alt: A render error in a widget bubbles up to the nearest error boundary. The boundary shows a fallback and reports the error, while the header, navigation and sibling panels keep working.

followUps: How do you catch an error thrown in an event handler?
How do you reset an error boundary after a retry?
How do error boundaries interact with Suspense?

questions.title: How do Suspense and React.lazy work together, and where do you place Suspense boundaries?
questions.quick: React.lazy wraps a dynamic import so a component's code loads on first render. While it loads, the component suspends, and the nearest Suspense boundary above it shows a fallback. I place boundaries at meaningful loading units such as routes and heavy panels rather than one at the root, so the rest of the page stays visible. Suspense also works with supporting data libraries and frameworks, which I would verify in current docs.
questions.revision: React.lazy suspends while its chunk loads; the nearest Suspense shows a fallback. Place boundaries at route and panel level.
questions.detailed:
**React.lazy** takes a function returning a dynamic import and gives back a component whose code is fetched the first time it renders. While the chunk is pending, the component **suspends**, and React shows the fallback of the nearest **Suspense** boundary. ```tsx const Reports = lazy(() => import('./Reports')); function App() { return ( Could not load reports.

}> }> ); } ``` {{diagram:susp}} ## Placement guidance | Boundary location | Effect | |---|---| | Root only | Whole screen flips to a spinner on any suspension | | Per route | Navigation shell stays; only the page area shows a fallback | | Per heavy panel | Independent panels load progressively | | Nested boundaries | Inner fallbacks show first, giving finer-grained loading | ## Good practice - Use **skeletons** that match the final layout to limit layout shift. - Wrap lazy components in an **error boundary**, because a failed chunk load throws. - Use a transition (startTransition or useTransition) so already visible content stays on screen instead of reverting to a fallback during navigation. - Prefetch likely next chunks on hover or idle, and avoid lazy-loading above-the-fold content that is needed for LCP. - Named exports need an adapter: import('./X').then(m => ({ default: m.X })). ## Version notes Suspense for data fetching, the use() API in React 19, and server component streaming depend on React version and framework. Treat these as framework-dependent and verify current docs. ## Common mistakes - Lazy-loading every component, creating waterfalls of tiny chunks. - No error boundary, so a network blip causes a blank page. - Calling lazy() inside a component body, which recreates the component every render. - Fallbacks with no reserved height, causing layout shifts.

diagrams.title: Lazy component and Suspense flow
diagrams.alt: On first render a lazy component starts a dynamic import and suspends. The nearest Suspense boundary shows its fallback. When the chunk arrives React renders the real component, and a failed load goes to the error boundary.

followUps: How do transitions avoid showing a fallback on navigation?
How would you prefetch a lazy route?
What happens if a chunk fails to load after a new deployment?

questions.title: useReducer vs useState: how do you decide?
questions.quick: I use useState for independent, simple values such as a toggle or an input. I switch to useReducer when several pieces of state change together, when the next state depends on the previous one in non-trivial ways, or when I want named actions that are easy to test and log. The reducer is a pure function, and dispatch is stable, which also helps when passing it through context.
questions.revision: useState for simple independent values; useReducer for related state, transitions and named actions in a pure, testable function.
followUps: Why does Strict Mode call reducers twice?
How would you pass dispatch through context safely?
When would you move from useReducer to a store library?

questions.title: When do you use useRef and useLayoutEffect, and how do they differ from useState and useEffect?
questions.quick: useRef holds a mutable value that survives renders without triggering one, so I use it for DOM nodes, timers and previous values. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM changes but before the browser paints, so I use it to measure layout and adjust before the user sees anything, such as positioning a tooltip. useEffect runs after paint and is the default. Because layout effects block painting, I keep them tiny.
questions.revision: useRef stores mutable values without re-rendering. useLayoutEffect runs before paint for measuring; useEffect runs after paint and is the default.

diagrams.title: Commit, layout effect, paint, effect order
diagrams.alt: After React commits DOM changes, layout effects run synchronously and can cause a synchronous re-render. Only then does the browser paint, and passive effects from useEffect run after the paint.

followUps: Why can useEffect cause a visible flicker for measurements?
How do you avoid layout thrashing in effects?
Why should you not write ref.current during render?

questions.title: What is a stale closure in React hooks, and how do dependency arrays prevent or cause it?
questions.quick: Every render creates new functions that capture that render's props and state. A stale closure happens when an effect, timer or callback keeps running an older function and sees old values. The dependency array tells React when to recreate the effect, so omitting a dependency is the usual cause. I fix it by listing the dependency, using the functional form setCount(c => c + 1), or keeping the latest value in a ref when I need a stable listener.
questions.revision: Each render captures its own values. Stale closures come from missing dependencies; fix with correct deps, functional updates or a ref.

diagrams.title: How a stale closure forms
diagrams.alt: Render one creates an effect whose callback captures the first value of state. Later renders create new callbacks with new values, but because the dependency array is empty the old callback stays registered and keeps reading the first value.

followUps: How does the functional form of setState avoid the problem?
Why does an inline object dependency re-run the effect every render?
How would you build a stable event listener that reads the latest props?

questions.title: How do you prevent race conditions and stale responses when fetching data in an effect?
questions.quick: If a query changes quickly, an older request can finish after a newer one and overwrite the screen with stale data. In an effect I create an AbortController, pass its signal to fetch, and abort in the cleanup function, ignoring AbortError. A boolean ignore flag also works for APIs that cannot be cancelled. In larger apps I prefer a server-state library that handles cancellation, caching and deduplication for me.
questions.revision: Cleanup aborts the previous request via AbortController, or sets an ignore flag, so a slow older response cannot overwrite newer state.

diagrams.title: Out-of-order responses
diagrams.alt: Request A for the old query is sent first and request B for the new query second. Response B arrives first, then slow response A arrives and overwrites state with stale data unless the cleanup function aborts request A.

followUps: Why is the double fetch in Strict Mode harmless with correct cleanup?
When is an ignore flag better than AbortController?
How would TanStack Query handle this for you?

questions.title: How does the lifecycle of a function component map to rendering, commit and effects?
questions.quick: A function component has three phases. Render calls my function to compute JSX and must be pure. Commit applies changes to the DOM, runs ref updates and layout effects. Then passive effects from useEffect run. On update the previous effect's cleanup runs before the next effect, and on unmount cleanups run. I do not map hooks one-to-one onto class lifecycles, because effects are about synchronisation with dependencies.
questions.revision: Render (pure), commit (DOM, refs, layout effects), then passive effects. Cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount.
questions.detailed:
Class lifecycles (componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, componentWillUnmount) are tied to **time**. Hooks are tied to **synchronisation**: an effect describes how to sync with something external for a given set of values. {{diagram:life}} ## Phases | Phase | What happens | Rules | |---|---|---| | Render | Component function runs, JSX returned | Must be pure; may run more than once (Strict Mode, concurrent rendering) | | Commit | DOM updated, refs attached, layout effects run | Synchronous | | Passive effects | useEffect callbacks run | After paint in most cases | | Update | Cleanup of previous effect, then new effect | Only if dependencies changed | | Unmount | Cleanups run, DOM removed | Release subscriptions | ## Rough class equivalents | Class | Function component | |---|---| | componentDidMount | useEffect(fn, []) (but think "sync once", and Strict Mode will run it twice in development) | | componentDidUpdate | useEffect(fn, [deps]) | | componentWillUnmount | cleanup returned from an effect | | getSnapshotBeforeUpdate | useLayoutEffect (partial) | | shouldComponentUpdate | React.memo | These are rough analogies. The mental model of "effect per dependency set" avoids bugs that the mount/update/unmount model invites. ## Example ```tsx function ChatRoom({ roomId }: { roomId: string }) { useEffect(() => { const conn = connect(roomId); // set up conn.join(); return () => conn.leave(); // tear down before next setup }, [roomId]); return

Room {roomId}

; } ``` When roomId changes, React leaves the old room, then joins the new one. ## Common mistakes - Doing side effects in the render body, such as writing to variables or calling APIs. - Believing a component renders only once per change. Renders can be repeated or discarded. - Using effects for derived values, which belong in render. - Skipping cleanup, which leaks listeners and timers.

diagrams.title: Function component lifecycle
diagrams.alt: A trigger such as new props or state starts a render phase that calls the function. React then commits to the DOM and runs layout effects, the browser paints, and finally passive effects run with earlier cleanups executed first.

questions.title: Container (smart) vs presentational components: is the pattern still useful with hooks?
questions.quick: Presentational components receive props and render UI, with little or no state of their own. Container components fetch data, hold state and pass it down. With hooks the split is less about separate files and more about separating concerns: put logic in custom hooks and keep the view dumb. I still keep rendering components free from data fetching, which makes them reusable, easy to test and easy to show in Storybook.
questions.revision: Presentational components render props; containers own data and logic. With hooks, extract logic into hooks and keep views pure.
followUps: How do server components change this pattern?

questions.title: How would you architect a large, multi-step form in React with validation?
questions.quick: I would use a form library such as react-hook-form, which registers inputs mostly as uncontrolled to avoid a render per keystroke, with a schema validator such as Zod shared with the server types. Each step is its own component and schema, values are kept in one form instance, and fields subscribe only to what they need. I validate on blur or submit, show accessible errors, persist drafts, and always re-validate on the server.
questions.revision: Use a form library with schema validation, one form state across step components, field-level subscriptions, accessible errors, drafts and server revalidation.

diagrams.title: Multi-step form architecture
diagrams.alt: A form provider holds values for all steps. Each step component registers its own fields and validates against its schema before advancing. On final submit the payload goes to the server, which revalidates and returns field errors that are mapped back to the form.

followUps: How do you validate across steps without losing data?
How would you handle dynamic field arrays?
How do you announce errors to screen reader users?

questions.title: What problems does a server-state library such as TanStack Query solve compared with fetching in effects?
questions.quick: Server state is remote data that can go stale, be shared and be changed by others. Fetching it in effects means I rebuild caching, deduplication, retries, loading flags, cancellation and invalidation by hand. A library such as TanStack Query keys each request, caches results, marks them stale after a configurable time, refetches in the background, deduplicates parallel calls, and supports mutations with invalidation or optimistic updates.
questions.revision: Server-state libraries give keyed caching, staleness, deduplication, retries, background refetch and mutation invalidation that effects do not.

diagrams.title: Server-state cache lifecycle
diagrams.alt: A component requests data by query key. If fresh data is cached it is returned immediately. If stale it is returned while a background refetch runs. A mutation invalidates matching keys so they refetch and update every subscribed component.

questions.title: How would you build and govern a shared React component library or design system for several teams?
questions.quick: I start from design tokens, then build accessible, themeable primitives and a small set of composed components, published as a versioned package with TypeScript types. Storybook documents each variant, tests cover behaviour and accessibility, and visual regression catches style drift. Governance matters as much as code: clear ownership, a contribution process, semantic versioning, deprecation policy and tree-shakeable builds so consumers do not pay for unused components.
questions.revision: Tokens, accessible primitives, versioned typed package, Storybook and visual tests, tree-shakeable builds, plus ownership and deprecation governance.

diagrams.title: Design system delivery flow
diagrams.alt: Design tokens feed accessible primitives, which are composed into higher-level components. These are documented in Storybook, verified by tests and visual regression, published as a versioned package, and consumed by product teams who feed requests back.

followUps: How do you version and deprecate components safely?
How do you keep the library tree-shakeable?
How do you measure design system adoption?
